title: Risk prediction in IgA nephropathy: from conventional models to machine learning, deep learning, and precision nephrology

paragraphs.en: Since its first description by Jean Berger and Nicole Hinglais in 1968 [1], IgA nephropathy (IgAN) has been recognized as the most common primary glomerular disease worldwide [2]. Its diagnosis relies on renal biopsy, which typically shows predominant or co-dominant IgA-containing immune complex deposits in the glomerular mesangium, with or without accompanying IgG or IgM deposits on immunofluorescence [3]. As a leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) [4], IgAN exhibits notable geographic variation in epidemiology. It is particularly prevalent in East Asian populations, accounting for 25–50% of primary glomerular diseases, while in Europe and North America, it accounts for about 15–30% [5]. The estimated global incidence is ∼2.5 cases per 100,000 people [6].

For clinicians, accurately evaluating the long-term risk of IgAN progression remains a significant challenge [7]. The disease course covers a broad range, from patients with persistent microscopic hematuria and minimal proteinuria who stay stable for decades, to those presenting with nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressing glomerulonephritis who advance to ESKD despite standard treatment [8]. Even among patients with seemingly similar clinical and pathological features, outcomes can vary greatly [9]. Approximately half of patients develop ESKD within 20 years [10], significantly impacting their quality of life and increasing healthcare costs. This prognostic uncertainty makes patient counseling, risk–benefit analysis, and treatment decisions more challenging, often leaving clinicians uncertain about when to intensify monitoring, initiate immunosuppression, or consider enrolling patients in clinical trials.

In this context, reliable prognostic prediction tools are critically needed to enable early identification of high-risk patients, guide personalized treatment plans, and optimize healthcare resource allocation. Over the past decades, the field has experienced a surge in prognostic modeling studies [11], driven by the increasing availability and integration of diverse data types, including clinical variables, histopathological features, and high-dimensional multi-omics profiles, as well as advances in modeling methodologies ranging from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning and deep learning techniques. Given the rapid pace and broad scope of these developments, a timely and comprehensive review is crucial to chart the evolution of models, identify emerging trends, and assess their potential for real-world clinical applications.

Previous reviews on prognostic modeling in IgA nephropathy have primarily focused on either traditional statistical methods or early machine learning applications, often providing descriptive overviews without thoroughly examining the methodological development and translational implications of these models [12]. In contrast, this review provides a comprehensive and current synthesis that covers the entire range of prognostic approaches. By comparing algorithmic designs, summarizing reported predictive performances, and critically examining key challenges such as interpretability, data heterogeneity, and regulatory readiness, our work connects methodological innovation with practical clinical use. It also highlights how next-generation, AI-powered prognostic tools could transform the future of precision nephrology and guide the development of clinical guidelines.

sections.title: Endpoints and risk factors in prognostic modeling of IgA nephropathy

paragraphs.en: The construction of prognostic models fundamentally depends on two elements: clearly defined endpoints and reliable predictive variables. In existing studies on IgAN, the most critical renal outcomes are often described as ‘hard endpoints’, usually referring to progression to ESKD, characterized by a sustained eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 or the initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT) [13,14]. Additionally, widely accepted surrogate endpoints, such as a ≥50% decline in eGFR from baseline [15], are used. These endpoints are clinically significant and directly indicate the risk of severe kidney dysfunction, making them central to most predictive models, which are often combined into composite renal outcomes [16–19].

Landmark indicators of ongoing disease activity, including 24-h urinary protein [20], urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) [21,22], eGFR slope [19,23,24] , serum creatinine [25], and time-averaged proteinuria [26], have also been used as endpoints because they detect subtle changes in kidney function that may indicate early disease progression. Importantly, specific thresholds for these endpoints are tailored to study populations and clinical settings: for example, several studies have defined eGFR decline thresholds ranging from 30 to 50% [27,28], annual eGFR loss from 2 to 5 mL/min/1.73 m2, and proteinuria thresholds between 0.3 and 0.5 g/day [29], depending on the study design.

The selection of predictive variables has evolved gradually as our understanding of IgAN has increased. Candidate predictors are typically based on previously identified risk factors and include clinical parameters, histopathological features, and multi-omics or biomarkers. Table 1 summarizes the endpoints and risk factors used in earlier studies, enabling clinicians to identify patient features strongly linked to clinical prognosis.

Classical predictive models for IgA nephropathy can be categorized into three main types based on their variables: models that utilize only pathological indicators, models based solely on clinical parameters, and models that incorporate clinical-pathological or omics-based variables. The emergence of these categories reflects researchers’ deep understanding of the disease’s pathological and clinical factors, while also illustrating how IgA nephropathy modeling has evolved by increasingly incorporating advances in omics technologies. To provide a clear overview, key prognostic models with significant clinical or methodological impact are summarized in Table 2, along with additional studies of interest in the Supplementary Table.

The development of pathology-based prediction models has progressively improved clinicians’ ability to assess patient risk and tailor treatment plans. Early research mostly focused on how different pathological classifications could predict outcomes. Yagame et al. [30] conducted a single-center study in Japan using a four-grade pathological classification system; over 15 years of follow-up, they found that patients with grade 4 severe lesions had a renal survival rate of only 22%, providing strong evidence for the predictive role of pathological damage in prognosis. Later, Radford et al. [46] carried out systematic, semi-quantitative evaluations of glomerular pathological changes in a U.S. patient group and proposed a ‘total glomerular score’ that combined four pathological features: glomerulosclerosis, capillary loop damage, cellular crescents, and fibrous adhesions. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that patients with scores above 5 had a significantly higher risk of ESKD, establishing clear therapeutic thresholds for clinical practice.

As the significance of pathological information in prognostic modeling became more evident, the traditional Lee classification system, with its complex five-grade structure, limited widespread clinical use. To address this issue, Manno et al. [47] conducted a single-center study in Italy and created a simplified three-tier histological grading system (mild, moderate, severe), demonstrating its better prognostic discrimination compared to the Lee classification. This development highlighted the need for effective prognostic tools to strike a balance between scientific accuracy and practicality in busy clinical settings.

The introduction of the Oxford classification marked a significant shift toward standardized and reproducible pathological assessment. Haaskjold et al. [31], using data from a Norwegian population, developed mathematical weighting algorithms that convert the complex MEST parameters into a single, clinically interpretable risk score. This innovation stratifies patients into four distinct risk categories, achieving predictive performance comparable to the full MEST system (15-year AUC: 0.85), thereby enabling clinicians to make informed treatment decisions without requiring extensive pathological expertise.

These developments collectively turn complex pathological data into actionable clinical insights, enabling nephrologists to optimize treatment plans, improve patient outcomes, and increase the accuracy of prognostic counseling in IgA nephropathy management.

In routine clinical practice, obtaining renal biopsy results can be challenging due to procedural risks, patient reluctance, and resource limitations. Recognizing this clinical reality, researchers have developed predictive models using readily available clinical parameters that can inform treatment decisions without the need for invasive procedures. In 1997, Frimat et al. [32] developed a practical three-tier prognostic classification system for male patients based on three easily accessible clinical parameters: serum creatinine, 24-h proteinuria, and gender. Following seven years of follow-up, this classification system demonstrated strong predictive capacity, providing clinicians with an immediate risk stratification tool bedside.

Building on earlier research, Bartosik et al. [33] recognized the value of including follow-up data to enhance predictive accuracy. They developed a prognostic model using mean arterial pressure (MAP) and protein excretion levels measured during follow-up, with the slope of the decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) as the primary endpoint. Multivariable linear regression analysis confirmed the model’s statistical significance (p < 0.001). This advancement enabled clinicians to adjust treatment intensity based on changing clinical trajectories, rather than relying solely on initial assessments, and fundamentally transformed how nephrologists monitor and respond to disease progression.

For the clinical management of aggressive IgA nephropathy, Lv et al. [34] developed a practical decision-support tool based on their finding that initial serum creatinine is the strongest predictor of outcome in crescentic cases. Using a univariate logistic regression model, they identified a clear prognostic threshold: when serum creatinine exceeds 6.8 mg/dL, patients have over a 90% chance of progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) within one year, with a specificity of 98.5%. This high-precision threshold allows clinicians to offer accurate prognostic counseling and make informed decisions about aggressive immunosuppressive therapy, timely transplant referral, and initiating palliative care discussions.

With the ongoing integration of predictive models into clinical practice, the study by Xie et al. [48] serves as a notable example. Conducted in China and validated externally in an independent Chinese cohort of over 1,200 patients, the authors demonstrated that a streamlined clinical model using only five routine parameters—age, gender, eGFR, hemoglobin, and proteinuria—achieved superior predictive performance (C-statistic: 0.86) compared to complex models that require histopathological data (C-statistic: 0.83). This finding indicates that comprehensive risk assessment can be performed using laboratory values available within hours of patient presentation, eliminating delays associated with biopsy scheduling, processing, and interpretation.

These noninvasive models are especially valuable in resource-limited settings, for elderly patients with comorbidities, and in situations where quick clinical decisions are crucial, offering clinicians worldwide effective prognostic tools that are both accessible and highly accurate.

sections.title: Predictive models incorporating combined clinical, pathological, and omics-based parameters

paragraphs.en: The importance of pathological indicators in IgA nephropathy has been increasingly confirmed, and more predictive modeling studies are trying to combine clinical and pathological features to achieve better prognostic accuracy. Wakai et al. [35] and Goto et al. [49] carried out follow-up studies based on cohorts of over 2,000 Japanese patients, creating a prognostic grading system that combined clinical indicators with pathological assessments at the time of biopsy. These models showed excellent prognostic prediction ability, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values over 0.92 in internal validation, confirming the strong predictive power of models that combine clinical and pathological data.

An early notable example of clinical translation was the Absolute Renal Risk (ARR) score proposed by Berthoux et al. [36]. Aiming for practical clinical use, this model sorts patients into four risk groups using only three variables easily available to nephrologists: hypertension status, proteinuria of 1 g/day, and severity of tissue damage. Despite its simple design, the ARR score proved to be highly useful, independently predicting dialysis or death with accuracy comparable to that of more complex multivariate models. This method filled an important gap between advanced statistical models and the real-world limits of clinical practice, although its dependence on non-standardized local pathological assessment criteria limited wider adoption.

The introduction of the Oxford Classification and its integration with clinical indicators opened new opportunities for prediction modeling. Tanaka et al. [37] integrated the Oxford Classification MEST indicators with clinical parameters (proteinuria and eGFR) to develop a novel risk prediction methodology, demonstrating excellent predictive efficacy in external validation (C-statistic = 0.89). This marked a crucial step toward creating prediction tools that could be reliably used across different clinical centers, effectively addressing challenges related to the generalizability of models in local contexts and specific populations (Japanese IgAN patients).

Recognizing the importance of developing prediction tools that work across different regions and ethnic groups for clinical decision-making, the International IgA Nephropathy Network, led by Barbour et al. [38], launched a large multinational collaboration. By combining data from nearly 4,000 patients across four continents, they created the International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool (IIgAN-PT), which uniquely combines clinical, pathological, and demographic features. The model’s strong external validation results (C-statistic: 0.82) and its broad applicability across populations and regions led to its endorsement as the preferred global risk assessment tool in the 2021 KDIGO guidelines [50]—a milestone that significantly changed clinical practice standards worldwide. To facilitate its clinical implementation, the model has also been deployed in several widely used online calculators and mobile applications, enabling convenient real-time risk estimation. In later research, Barbour et al. [40] continued to refine this model to enable precise risk reassessment 1–2 years after biopsy. Additionally, using modeling strategies and parameter adjustments similar to those employed in the IIgAN-PT, the team successfully adapted the model for pediatric populations [39], further refining its parameters to enable accurate risk reevaluation 1–2 years post-biopsy in children [41]. These efforts expanded its clinical usefulness across age groups and provided nephrologists with an evidence-based tool to better manage this particularly challenging patient group.

While the IIgAN-PT has transformed routine clinical practice worldwide, the exploration of IgA nephropathy prognostic prediction continues to expand into broader predictive areas and more advanced clinical applications. Currently, nomogram-based models are beginning to address clinical situations that were previously overlooked in prognostic modeling. These include predicting outcomes in IgA nephropathy patients who develop acute kidney injury [51], a complication with significant treatment implications, and estimating short-term (90-day) outcomes [52], which are crucial for guiding early clinical interventions. These advances, along with models that incorporate new risk factors [53–55], have transformed complex statistical analyses into visual risk assessment tools, providing clinicians with actionable insights and enhancing the accuracy of personalized patient care.

Currently, the integration of advanced modeling algorithms and omics technologies is the next frontier in clinically relevant prognostic prediction. Le et al. [56] pioneered the use of joint modeling techniques, combining longitudinal data of key clinical parameters (eGFR and proteinuria) with time-to-event outcomes to better capture the dynamic nature of patient prognosis—an approach that significantly improved model performance, as shown by the increase in AUC from 0.864 at biopsy to 0.95 after five years of follow-up. This dynamic method not only more accurately mirrors real-world clinical practice but also marks a meaningful step toward extending traditional prognostic models for real-time prediction of IgA nephropathy outcomes. At the same time, biomarker-based models using renal tissue complement components [42], kidney injury-specific urinary indicators [43], metabolomics-derived blood and urine metabolites [44], and urinary chemokines [45] have achieved AUC scores near or above 0.90. These progressions highlight the potential of molecular markers to improve prognostic accuracy in IgA nephropathy, with clinically applicable biomarker panels set to provide unprecedented precision, enable earlier and more personalized treatments, and ultimately enhance patient outcomes.

While classical prognostic models have transformed risk assessment from empirical clinical judgment to evidence-based methods, they still have certain limitations when used in real-world therapeutic decision-making. Traditional Cox regression models, for example, rely on a limited set of predetermined variables and assume linear relationships, often failing to capture the complex, multifactorial nature of disease progression that clinicians observe in practice. This limitation becomes especially problematic when determining optimal treatment intensity, timing of immunosuppressive therapy, or counseling patients about long-term renal outcomes. These structural constraints of regression-based approaches highlight an urgent need for more flexible modeling strategies that can handle nonlinear interactions and high-dimensional clinical data. Machine learning algorithms utilize the full range of available clinical information—from routine lab parameters to histopathological findings—to identify subtle prognostic differences that traditional statistical methods miss. These data-driven approaches excel at processing complex, high-dimensional datasets that accurately reflect the multifaceted clinical reality of IgA nephropathy, thereby addressing the shortcomings of conventional predictive models. Such approaches may provide clinicians with more nuanced and personalized risk-stratification tools, supporting informed therapeutic decision-making and potentially enhancing patient outcomes. To provide a comprehensive overview, all machine learning–based prognostic studies discussed in this review are summarized in Table 3, allowing direct comparison of model design, predictive variables, clinical endpoints, and performance.

sections.title: Single machine learning algorithm modeling for prediction

paragraphs.en: Geddes et al. [57] conducted the initial study on applying machine learning for prognostic predictions in IgA nephropathy. They developed an artificial neural network (ANN) using six routine clinical variables to predict whether serum creatinine would reach a level of ≥150 μmol/L after seven years. The model achieved an accuracy of 87.0%, significantly surpassing the 69.4% accuracy of experienced nephrologists. This pioneering research demonstrated both the feasibility and the clinical potential of machine learning–based prognostic models in IgA nephropathy.

Following the confirmation of machine learning’s viability in this field, subsequent research has explored various machine learning algorithms within Asian populations. For instance, Goto et al. [58] employed a decision tree to classify patients by their 10-year risk of renal failure. They utilized six clinical variables to assign patients into seven risk categories, with renal impairment rates from 1.0% to 51.4%. The model demonstrated a discriminative power comparable to logistic regression (AUC: 0.830 vs. 0.808), reinforcing the potential of machine learning for risk stratification.

Early machine learning prediction models often faced challenges in being adopted in clinical practice. It was not until 2013 that Di Noia et al. [59] developed the m-IgAN model, an ANN-based framework utilizing single-center data from Italy, marking the first machine learning model for IgAN prognosis to be clinically applied. This model achieved 89.1% accuracy and was designed to be user-friendly as a clinical decision support system (CDSS), enabling nephrologists to input patient data and receive instant risk assessments during consultations. Building on this, Pesce et al. [60] combined multicenter data from Italy, Norway, and Japan to create two ANN models with six predictors, estimating both the occurrence and timing of ESKD. The models achieved AUC values from 89.9 to 100% across three national cohorts for ESKD prediction. For timing predictions, F1-scores exceeded 70% in all cohorts. Both models outperformed traditional absolute renal risk scores and nephrologists’ assessments, demonstrating that the tool could reliably maintain accuracy across various healthcare settings and populations, thus establishing a foundation for applying machine learning predictive models in clinical practice.

Subsequently, Schena et al. [61] conducted ANN-based modeling research with a strong focus on predictor interpretability and standardized evaluation methods. They used Cox regression to identify seven independent risk factors and built an ANN model using data from 758 patients, with the remaining data reserved for both internal and external validation. The model achieved 91% accuracy on an independent external validation cohort (European population), outperforming other ANN models and CDSS systems. This study not only demonstrates that combining statistical feature selection with machine learning modeling is an effective approach to achieving high generalizability but also helps alleviate clinicians’ concerns about the ‘black-box’ nature of such models to some extent.

However, developing robust and highly generalizable models remains difficult. Kim et al. [62] created and validated a random forest model using data from two centers in a Korean population to predict the short-term progression of IgA nephropathy. The model trained on data from one center performed nearly perfectly in the validation cohort (AUROC = 0.993), but its performance dropped significantly when tested externally with data from the other center (AUROC = 0.771). This sharp decline indicates overfitting and makes otherwise high-performing models unreliable for clinical use. This study suggests that, despite the apparent impressiveness of internal validation metrics, they cannot replace thorough external validation. Only models that demonstrate strong performance across diverse patient groups and healthcare settings should be considered suitable for routine clinical use.

With the rapid advancement of machine learning algorithms, numerous studies have employed various modeling methods to compare predictions for the same targets, aiming to maximize algorithmic predictive advantages. Diciolla et al. [63] combined multicenter data from Italy, Norway, and Japan to systematically compare the predictive performance of artificial neural networks (ANN), neuro-fuzzy systems (NFS), support vector machines (SVM), and decision trees, pioneering algorithm comparison studies in IgA nephropathy (IgAN). Their results showed that ANN performed best in predicting progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within five years after biopsy (F1 > 0.9), confirming the robustness of ANN across multicenter datasets. However, the study also indicates that the effect of data imbalance on predictive reliability needs careful attention in clinical use.

Chen et al. [64] further refined and expanded this approach by establishing and comparing ten prognostic models for IgA nephropathy, identifying XGBoost as the top-performing model (C-index: 0.84). They also extracted key predictors—proteinuria, global glomerulosclerosis, and interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy (IFTA)—to develop a simplified scoring model (SSM), improving clinical usefulness for risk stratification. Similarly, Han et al. [65] compared six algorithms and found that although logistic regression achieved the highest AUC value (96.1%), random forest was the preferred method for IgA nephropathy prediction due to its better balance of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. In 2020, Zhang et al. [66] identified the unique challenges in pediatric nephrology, confirmed the excellent performance of the XGBoost model (AUC = 0.851) through a multi-algorithm comparison, and developed an online prediction platform using the Django framework, enabling personalized management in pediatric patients. Overall, these studies not only confirmed the predictive power of ANN but also showed the benefits of ensemble learning methods in IgAN prognostic modeling.

Although most current research generally emphasizes the advantages of machine learning over traditional models, the modeling study by Park et al. [67] provides a cautionary example. Using multicenter data from South Korea, they developed multiple machine learning and deep learning models and compared them to the traditional IIgAN-PT model. They found that, despite good performance in predicting ESKD risk, these advanced models did not show a statistically significant improvement over the established international IgA nephropathy prediction tool. More concerning from a clinical safety standpoint, some models tended to underestimate risk, which could lead to inadequate monitoring of patients at high risk. This study suggests that sophisticated modeling techniques do not automatically outperform classical approaches. Improvements in model performance should be based on predictive accuracy, clinical interpretability, and practical usefulness, rather than on mere ‘technical complexity’. Building on this, Hirano et al. [68] proposed creating adaptive IgAN prognostic models tailored to different healthcare levels. They recommended that lower-level hospitals use simple predictive models with fewer variables, while higher-level academic centers adopt machine learning models that include a wider range of available predictors. Their comparison of logistic regression and four other machine learning algorithms ultimately identified the LightGBM model as performing best in the validation cohort (C-statistic = 0.802), balancing accuracy and stability.

Together, these studies have accelerated the development of machine learning–based prognostic models for IgAN, demonstrating their predictive benefits while also highlighting the need to consider the black-box effects and potential risks they may pose.

With ongoing advances in machine learning and the deep integration of artificial intelligence with systems biology, prognostic prediction research in IgAN is entering a transformative phase. The focus has shifted from merely optimizing existing algorithms or combining traditional clinical data to two main directions: developing new algorithms and integrating multi-omics data.

Regarding algorithm innovation, Li et al. [69] combined the nonlinear fitting capabilities of XGBoost with time-dependent frameworks in survival analysis, thereby developing the XGBoost-Surv model. This model demonstrated exceptional predictive performance in external validation among the Chinese population (time-dependent C-index = 0.822), significantly surpassing traditional and other machine learning survival models. Through SHAP interpretability analysis and model encapsulation, the study further explored practical pathways for clinical translation. Ying, Yaozhe et al. [70,71] integrated swarm intelligence optimization algorithms with support vector machines and k-nearest neighbor algorithms to build predictive models tailored for patients with varying levels of proteinuria. These models achieved nearly 99% accuracy on specific datasets, highlighting the great potential of algorithmic innovation for specific application scenarios.

In the field of multi-omics data fusion, Rudnicki et al. [72] used urinary proteomic data to develop the ‘IgAN237’ classifier with SVM algorithms. When combined with clinical parameters, its ability to predict rapid disease progression improved significantly, with the AUC increasing from 0.72 to 0.89, emphasizing the importance of noninvasive prognostic assessment. Tan, Jiaxing et al. [73] viewed patients as complex biological networks, integrating multi-omics data and using autoencoders to extract deep features. They created an unsupervised learning–based network biomarker clustering model (KMN) that not only outperformed the internationally recognized IIgAN-PT tool in predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.77) but also effectively identified patient subgroups likely to benefit from immunosuppressive therapy, reflecting a growing trend toward moving from simple prognostic predictions to more detailed and comprehensive assessments.

sections.title: Strengths and limitations of machine learning algorithms

paragraphs.en: A wide range of ML algorithms have been used in IgAN prognostic modeling, each with distinct algorithmic features that influence their suitability for specific clinical data situations. Tree-based ensemble methods such as RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are especially useful for structured tabular data that includes both categorical and continuous variables. Their advantages include clear interpretability through feature importance ranking, resilience to outliers, and strong performance with moderate-sized datasets. However, they are limited by their sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning and their inability to model temporal data, which restricts their use in dynamic prediction [74].

Support Vector Machines (SVM) and k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) models are effective for small to medium-sized datasets with clear class separation. SVMs perform well with high-dimensional data and non-linear boundaries using kernel functions, but they struggle with large-scale datasets and the calibration of probabilistic outputs [75]. KNN, while straightforward, can suffer from overfitting and poor generalization when irrelevant features or noisy variables are present [76].

Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) provide flexibility in modeling complex non-linear relationships between clinical and pathological predictors. Their advantages include capturing hidden feature interactions and supporting multi-task learning [77]. However, ANN models typically require large datasets and careful regularization to prevent overfitting, and their ‘black box’ nature reduces interpretability without additional techniques such as SHAP or LIME [78].

Hybrid and meta-learning frameworks, such as model ensembles or swarm intelligence–optimized classifiers, improve prediction stability by combining different algorithmic approaches. Their strength is in merging complementary learning biases, but they also increase computational complexity and reduce transparency [79]. Overall, these algorithmic variations show that choosing an ML method should depend more on the data type, sample size, and intended clinical use case rather than on algorithmic sophistication alone.

The continuous advances in algorithm development and multi-omics data integration are turning traditional ‘black-box’ predictive models into smarter systems that can elucidate underlying biological mechanisms, enable dynamic risk assessment, and guide personalized approaches to treatment [80]. However, as these data-driven methods become more widely used in clinical research, it is essential to address the ongoing challenge of overfitting, which can compromise the reliability and generalizability of models. Overfitting often occurs when the sample size is too small to capture true population diversity or when noise and irrelevant information are unintentionally included during training [81]. Therefore, careful assessment of data quality and model inputs is essential for creating reliable and clinically useful prognostic tools. In this setting, finding the right balance between model complexity, data quality, and biological interpretability will be crucial to ensure that machine learning–based systems ultimately deliver their intended value in managing IgA nephropathy.

The ongoing progress of deep learning, especially its core ability in representation learning, enables the automatic extraction of hierarchical features from unstructured data, including pathological images and longitudinal follow-up records. By overcoming the limitations of traditional structured data approaches, these methods broaden the scope of prognostic research in IgA nephropathy and help identify patterns previously unnoticed within routinely collected clinical and biopsy data. This offers the potential to enhance personalized risk stratification and guide clinical decision-making. Table 4 provides an overview of emerging deep learning–driven prognostic models for IgAN, serving as a reference point for ongoing innovation and potential clinical application.

sections.title: Development of deep learning in prognostic prediction of IgA nephropathy

paragraphs.en: Testa et al. [82] developed a deep learning prediction score (DLPS) model based on CNN architecture that predicts kidney failure using only whole slide images (WSI) from renal biopsies, achieving an AUC of 0.84. Importantly for practicing pathologists, this study also highlighted the significant prognostic value of inflammatory infiltration in regions of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (i-IFTA). A subsequent multicenter study by Cho et al. [83] further validated the prognostic potential of deep pathological image information, employing the DeepLabV3Plus and EfficientNet-B3 models for automated glomerular segmentation and classification. The XGBoost model built from these image features demonstrated exceptional performance in predicting adverse kidney outcomes with an AUC of 0.941, comparable to composite models that incorporate extensive clinical variables.

Beyond a detailed exploration of pathological structures, the dynamic assessment of disease progression in patients also provides valuable information for prognosis. Chen et al. [84] developed an interpretable multivariate LSTM (IMV-LSTM) that reflects how clinicians actually monitor patients over time. By combining baseline static variables with time-varying follow-up data—such as eGFR, proteinuria, and blood pressure—the model enables dynamic prediction of kidney outcomes. External validation in a Chinese population yielded a C-statistic of 0.93, significantly surpassing traditional models based solely on initial data (C-statistic = 0.79). This approach enables models to more accurately identify patients who may require more aggressive treatment from those who can be safely monitored, which is crucial in nephrology practice.

Addressing the practical need for comprehensive clinical workflow integration, Pan et al. [85] developed a deep sequential neural network (DeepSNN) system that automates the entire diagnostic and prognostic prediction process—from initial lesion segmentation and glomerular classification through standardized Oxford MEST-C scoring to final outcome prediction. This end-to-end approach directly improves workflow efficiency in busy clinical settings. In Oxford classification tasks, DeepSNN performance approached that of senior pathologists, while in prognostic prediction, it achieved an AUC of 0.810, significantly higher than the IIgAN-PT model (AUC = 0.742), potentially enabling more accurate treatment stratification in routine clinical practice.

The use of deep learning algorithms has demonstrated that, within standard diagnostic workflows and routine monitoring data, they can identify clinically useful patterns and provide nephrologists with enhanced decision support that integrates seamlessly into current practices. Further development of deep learning could enhance more accurate measurements of subtle pathological features and better tracking of disease progression over time, helping to reduce diagnostic uncertainty and improve treatment timing. However, the ‘black box’ nature of deep learning remains a significant challenge for clinical use, as it hampers trust and adoption because clinicians cannot verify the biological basis of the model’s predictions [86]. There is a pressing need for interpretable deep learning methods, such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and attention mechanisms, which highlight the features influencing the model’s decisions, like pathological structures or key data points over time [87,88]. Balancing predictive accuracy with clinical interpretability is crucial for the successful integration of this approach into routine nephrology practice. Despite this, DL-based systems, which offer dynamic time-series predictions rather than static baseline estimates, represent a promising advancement toward real-time, adaptive risk monitoring in clinical nephrology.

sections.title: Strengths and limitations of deep learning architectures

paragraphs.en: Each deep learning architecture presents unique advantages and challenges for clinical application. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are highly effective at recognizing spatial patterns and extracting morphological features, making them especially useful for digital pathology and whole-slide image analysis [89]. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models excel at handling sequential or longitudinal data, such as serial eGFR, proteinuria, or blood pressure records, supporting dynamic time-series predictions [90]. Hybrid sequential neural networks (DeepSNNs) and multimodal frameworks combine imaging, clinical, and laboratory data to provide comprehensive patient-level risk assessments [91]. However, these models typically require large, well-annotated datasets and substantial computational resources for training. Additionally, they are prone to overfitting and can be difficult to interpret without the use of explainability techniques, such as attention visualization or gradient attribution [92]. The key to successful implementation in real-world nephrology practice lies in striking a balance between model complexity, interpretability, and clinical practicality.

sections.title: Comparing and advancing prognostic models in IgA nephropathy

paragraphs.en: Although significant progress has been made in prognostic modeling, a unified framework for systematically comparing the theoretical foundations of different approaches is still missing. Furthermore, the diversity of existing models presents a major challenge in accurately assessing their real-world clinical usefulness. More importantly, most previous modeling studies have been done in isolation, without establishing a clear translational pathway from algorithm development to practice, which is an essential component of the clinical translation of machine learning models. Addressing these issues will enable a more critical and rigorous evaluation of new predictive models, supporting their proper selection and application in relevant clinical settings.

The differences among various types of prognostic model development mainly relate to how risk is represented and inferred. Classical models typically view disease progression as a static function of baseline covariates, incorporating these variables into predictions through predefined parametric relationships [93]. In contrast, machine learning models identify complex nonlinear interactions within structured data [94], while deep learning further expands data dimensionality by extracting hierarchical representations directly from unstructured inputs [95]. These differences are not just methodological; they also reflect different epistemological assumptions about disease biology and clinical decision-making. Despite their apparent differences, when viewed through the data–model–action framework (Figure 1), these three modeling approaches share core similarities. Each one critically depends on the quality and representativeness of data as its foundation. Classical models need carefully selected variables with established clinical relevance; machine learning algorithms rely on large enough sample sizes to prevent overfitting in expanded feature spaces; and deep learning models require massive, well-annotated datasets to tune millions of parameters. This reliance highlights a universal limitation: no modeling method can surpass the limits of its training data. This principle shows that a model’s performance is inherently limited by the informational value of its training data, as explained in statistical learning theory through the concept of generalization bounds.

At the algorithmic level, these paradigms differ most noticeably, reflecting different strategies for extracting predictive signals from data. Classical models depend on parametric assumptions (e.g., proportional hazards or linearity in log-odds space) [96]. Machine learning approaches utilize ensemble methods and recursive partitioning [97], whereas deep learning operates through gradient-based optimization across highly non-convex objective landscapes [98]. Despite these differences, all these methods share a common goal: minimizing prediction error while maintaining some form of model simplicity or regularization.

Ultimately, all modeling trajectories tend to focus on the ‘action’ part within the data–model–action triad. No matter how advanced the algorithm, the value of a predictive model is not judged by its mathematical elegance or computational novelty, but by its ability to guide therapeutic decisions, adjust treatment levels, support patient counseling, and ultimately improve clinical results. This practical goal remains consistent across different modeling approaches, underscoring that while methodological improvements are important, they are secondary to the primary aim of gaining actionable clinical insights.

Evaluating predictive performance is a crucial step in determining whether a prediction model can be widely applied. Historically, most modeling studies have relied on performance discrimination metrics, such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) or the C-statistic, as primary indicators of model quality. While these measures facilitate cross-study comparisons, they are not the sole criteria for evaluating the overall quality of a predictive model [99]. Given the high-risk nature of clinical decision-making and prognosis assessment, predictive models must strike a balance between interpretability and accuracy. Additionally, considering economic differences among regions, a model’s generalizability and accessibility form a third important aspect, known as usability. Therefore, the assessment of prediction models should thoroughly include interpretability, usability, and predictive performance as the three core dimensions.

Although usability and interpretability are distinct conceptual aspects, they both influence the clinical acceptability of predictive models. However, as model complexity increases, the quality of both tends to decline. The practical feasibility of deploying a model primarily depends on data requirements, computational demands, and its ability to integrate seamlessly into existing clinical workflows. Classical prediction models generally demonstrate high usability, as they rely solely on standard clinical variables, require minimal computational resources, and can be easily integrated into nephrology workflows, aligning with the ‘low-burden intervention’ principle emphasized in implementation science.

In contrast, the rapid progress of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) has led to models that require more complex and expensive inputs, such as detailed proteomic panels, GPU-accelerated infrastructure for real-time inference, or digitized pathology data produced by specific scanner specifications. These resource-intensive requirements significantly limit the usability of these models in various healthcare settings, contributing to the slow clinical adoption of such technologies.

Furthermore, unlike traditional models with transparent mathematical structures, ML and DL models, while providing better predictive accuracy, often lack straightforward interpretability. This lack of transparency reduces clinicians’ willingness to depend on them for decision-making. The rise of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has partially addressed this issue by introducing post-hoc interpretation methods such as SHAP values, LIME, and attention mechanisms. These techniques help boost clinicians’ trust in model predictions. However, current interpretability methods still encounter problems, including instability and the potential for misrepresentation of the model’s actual reasoning [100]. When a model’s internal logic cannot be clearly understood, it should not be used in high-stakes clinical settings, regardless of its accuracy [101]. This approach is consistent with the broader regulatory shift toward algorithmic accountability, as highlighted by the GDPR rules and the U.S. FDA’s increasing oversight of medical AI systems [102–104].

In the development of prognostic models for IgA nephropathy, a pattern of diminishing returns in performance improvements has been noted. This suggests that as our understanding of disease mechanisms deepens, model performance may be approaching an intrinsic upper limit set by the stochastic nature of disease progression, rather than algorithmic limitations. Incremental gains, although statistically significant, often have limited clinical usefulness [105]. Additionally, apparent improvements in some studies might result from overfitting or methodological artifacts rather than genuine advances in predictive accuracy [106]. Therefore, moving from single-center, small-sample, coarse-grained datasets to multicenter, multiethnic, large-scale, and carefully curated datasets is crucial for developing more robust and generalizable prediction models.

In summary, prognostic prediction models should be evaluated through a multidimensional approach, rather than focusing solely on maximizing predictive accuracy. Drawing from the evaluation framework proposed by Tan et al. [107], this review assesses the included prediction models based on usability, interpretability, and predictive performance, each rated on a 10-point scale. Higher total scores reflect greater overall utility. Table 5 details the scoring criteria, with each dimension divided into four subcomponents to ensure a thorough assessment. As shown in Table 6, the two multicenter studies conducted by Barbour et al. received the highest scores, highlighting the strong potential of their models for global clinical use.

In the field of prognostic modeling for IgA nephropathy (IgAN), the real challenge isn’t the complexity of the algorithms themselves but how to ensure these models can truly operate in clinical practice. Moving from ‘predictable’ to ‘actionable’ demands a systematic translational framework that combines model development, validation, and implementation into an ongoing, integrated process. To achieve this, we propose a comprehensive roadmap (Figure 2) that serves as a structured guide for the future development and deployment of IgAN prognostic models.

This process starts with a strong data foundation. Only by establishing high-quality, standardized, and privacy-aware multicenter collaborative cohorts can we address the current issues of small sample sizes and high data variability that affect the reproducibility and broad applicability of our findings. Combining cross-institutional and multimodal data, including clinical, pathological, and molecular information, provides a realistic and comprehensive basis for model input, creating favorable conditions for future generalization and validation. An open yet regulated data governance system not only protects patient privacy but also promotes international data sharing, turning model development from isolated lab efforts into a collaborative research network.

Building on this, the focus of model development is shifting from static and closed predictive systems to dynamic, interpretable, and generative artificial intelligence frameworks. The next generation of models should be able to track the long-term progression of disease by integrating time-based features and multimodal signals, enabling real-time risk estimation. Simultaneously, interpretability is crucial for gaining clinical trust and usability. By using explainable AI frameworks and generative modeling techniques, predictions become not just algorithmic outputs but understandable insights that clinicians can interpret and verify. This is a crucial step toward transforming algorithms into reliable tools for clinical decision support.

However, scientific rigor alone does not automatically ensure clinical value. The key turning point is in thorough multidimensional validation. Besides confirming predictive accuracy in independent groups, it’s essential to assess model fairness and relevance across different populations and clinical environments. External validation, evaluation of clinical usefulness, and prospective impact studies should be fundamental parts of future research. Only when a model shows clear benefits for clinical decision-making and patient outcomes in real-world practice can it be considered a truly actionable prognostic tool.

Ultimately, the goal of this translational pathway is not only the model itself, but also its seamless integration into clinical workflows. The model should be integrated into electronic health records and intelligent decision-support systems, enabling physicians to participate in a human-AI collaborative decision-making process. At the same time, following regulatory frameworks like FDA guidelines and Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), along with ongoing monitoring of model performance, will ensure safety, reliability, and sustainability in patient care. Through this systematic approach—from high-quality data foundations, to adaptable and interpretable model development, to multidimensional validation and clinical integration—IgAN prognostic research is moving toward the era of precision nephrology, ultimately aiming for personalized disease management and better patient outcomes.

sections.title: Challenges and future prospects of prognostic prediction models for IgA nephropathy

paragraphs.en: Over the past thirty years, prognostic models for IgA nephropathy (IgAN) have quietly reshaped clinical practice. They have shifted from relying on subjective clinical judgment to evidence-based risk stratification. Recently, these models have become more advanced and comprehensive, utilizing intelligent prediction algorithms. This progress helps tackle a key challenge in nephrology: identifying high-risk patients within the diverse IgAN population and determining the best timing for interventions to prevent irreversible kidney damage. Despite this advancement, such research has significant implications for clinical decision support, model regulatory approval, establishing frameworks for cross-disease prognostic evaluation, assessing the predictive power of new therapies, and informing future guidelines. Yet, many obstacles remain before these models can be widely adopted and thoroughly validated.

sections.title: Clinical decision implications of predictive tools

paragraphs.en: Predictive models are becoming more influential in clinical decision-making for IgAN. Dynamic risk estimation helps determine when and if to perform a renal biopsy, especially in patients with mild urinary abnormalities or early eGFR decline, where invasive procedures can be postponed unless the risk of progression is high. Likewise, risk trajectories from ML- and DL-based tools can guide the optimal timing for initiating or discontinuing immunosuppressive therapy, thereby reducing unnecessary exposure in low-risk patients and identifying those likely to benefit from early treatment. Additionally, predictive algorithms support risk-based patient stratification for clinical trial enrollment, ensuring those with a higher chance of progression are prioritized, which improves trial efficiency and the accuracy of therapeutic assessments. As these models develop and integrate into electronic health record systems, data-driven, risk-adjusted decision-making will increasingly enhance precision nephrology within everyday clinical workflows.

From a regulatory perspective, deploying AI-based prognostic tools in clinical settings requires compliance with evolving standards from agencies like the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA). Issues related to algorithm traceability, data provenance, model version control, and performance drift must be managed within the framework of Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP). Transparent validation pipelines, external benchmarking, and ongoing post-market surveillance will be crucial to ensure safety, reproducibility, and long-term clinical reliability. Furthermore, establishing effective physician oversight and human-in-the-loop governance mechanisms will be crucial for maintaining clinician trust and ensuring patient safety as AI models transition from research to regulated clinical use.

sections.title: Prognostic models in the era of emerging therapies

paragraphs.en: With the rapid emergence of new therapies for IgA nephropathy, such as targeted-release budesonide, complement inhibitors including iptacopan and narsoplimab, as well as factor B inhibitors and endothelin receptor antagonists, the role of prognostic models is expected to expand from risk assessment to guiding treatment decisions. Baseline risk stratification tools, like the International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool (IIgAN-PT), along with integrated clinicopathologic and biomarker-based models, can help identify high-risk patients who are likely to benefit from these new treatments and support patient selection strategies in clinical trials. Additionally, mechanism-focused biomarkers, especially those indicating complement activation in kidney tissue or urine, may serve as predictive markers for choosing candidates for complement-targeted therapies. Simultaneously, dynamic prediction frameworks that incorporate longitudinal eGFR and proteinuria trends (such as joint modeling or LSTM-based approaches) offer an opportunity to track early treatment responses and adjust therapies in real time, using surrogate endpoints like proteinuria reduction or eGFR slope stabilization. Future studies should prospectively validate these combined models in biomarker-defined groups and assess their clinical usefulness through calibration, discrimination, and decision-curve analyses, thereby enabling precise application of emerging therapies and enhancing personalized care in IgA nephropathy.

sections.title: Impact on KDIGO and future guideline updates

paragraphs.en: The integration of the International IgA Nephropathy Prediction Tool (IIgAN-PT) into the 2021 KDIGO guidelines marked a significant milestone in evidence-based risk assessment. This achievement reflected the growing recognition that quantitative, reproducible prediction models can inform treatment choices and improve patient outcomes. As machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL)-based dynamic models show better long-term performance and adaptability to changing patient data, future guideline updates are likely to officially recognize AI-enabled tools as supportive instruments for clinical decision-making. Including these tools could transform standard care by encouraging data-driven decisions on biopsy timing, personalized immunosuppression plans, and tailored follow-up schedules. Over time, risk-based algorithms could become essential parts of KDIGO recommendations for managing both adult and pediatric IgA nephropathy.

Despite remarkable progress, several research gaps need to be filled before predictive tools can be fully integrated into real-world nephrology practice. Future research should focus on the following key priorities:

Cross-ethnic and multicenter validation: Developed primarily in East Asian cohorts, current models require thorough multicenter testing in non-Asian populations to ensure their applicability and fairness globally.
Dynamic time-series prediction: integrating longitudinal trajectories (e.g., eGFR and proteinuria) for real-time risk recalibration.
Federated and privacy-preserving learning: enabling collaborative model training across institutions while maintaining data security.
Model interpretability: enhancing transparency with explainable AI methods like SHAP values, attention mechanisms, and saliency mapping.
Regulatory and deployment readiness: aligning with FDA and Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) frameworks to ensure clinical-grade robustness.

Integration of digital pathology: deep learning models can now directly extract prognostically relevant glomerular features from whole-slide images, underscoring the growing clinical value of AI-driven pathology.

Emerging generative AI applications: diffusion and transformer-based models may facilitate data augmentation, phenotype simulation, and uncertainty-aware prediction, speeding up precision risk stratification and tailored therapy planning in IgAN.

The ongoing evolution of predictive modeling in IgAN exemplifies how AI-driven analytics can fundamentally reshape prognostic assessment in complex glomerular diseases. Recent deep learning frameworks have demonstrated the clinical value of digital pathology, with convolutional and attention-based models extracting prognostic glomerular features directly from whole-slide images [108,109]. The next generation of prognostic tools is expected to integrate clinical parameters, pathology, omics, and longitudinal trajectories through multimodal fusion architectures. Emerging generative AI techniques, such as diffusion models, may enable data augmentation, phenotype simulation, and uncertainty-aware forecasting, accelerating precision risk stratification and individualized treatment planning in IgAN. The conceptual and methodological advances summarized in this review may serve as a reference framework for developing and validating prognostic tools in related conditions such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), membranous nephropathy (MN), and lupus nephritis (LN). By integrating deep learning, digital pathology, multimodal omics, and dynamic time-series modeling, next-generation systems are poised to deliver continuously updated, individualized, and interpretable prognostic insights. Ultimately, such innovations will enable a paradigm shift from static, one-time risk estimation toward real-time, adaptive prediction, bringing precision nephrology closer to practical reality.

The information presented in this table adheres to strict data extraction and prioritization criteria to ensure maximum comparability and rigor.

1. Reported metric: Model discrimination was primarily assessed and reported using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) or the C-statistic (C-index), as available in the source literature.

2. Optimal model: In studies where comparative analysis of multiple predictive models was conducted, only the performance metrics of the algorithm demonstrating the highest predictive performance were included.

3. Temporal scope: When a model provided performance metrics for different time-to-event outcomes, the metric corresponding to the model with the longest prediction follow-up period was selected for representation.

4. Validation hierarchy: The reported performance data were strictly prioritized based on the robustness of the validation technique, favoring more rigorous methods: External Validation was prioritized over Internal Validation (e.g., internal cross-validation or bootstrapping), which was favored over models with no formal validation method.
